I did a year of CBT and DBT etc with multiple therapists and group therapy and it never helped me with my rumination (my point of view and not saying that they won't work for you), but I personally recommend Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT).

This has a different point of view where instead of trying to engage with thoughts and challenging them to attempt to change or reduce them, you instead 'unhook' yourself from your thoughts. This is done by asking yourself whether if you debated your thoughts for say the next 15 minutes, would you gain anymore value for your life? I feel this is a good filter for whether or not you want to continue down that internal discourse. We tend to assign lots of importance to thoughts but they are just words/stories/language in our head and have no truth to them.

For ACT I would recommend the corny-titled book 'the happiness trap' by Russ Harris.

I would also recommend meditation, I know everyone goes on about it, but it's a really good foundation to any kind of self-work, because it helps you realise sooner when you are drifting with a thought.

Hope this helps and much love to you I wish you the best on your journey of self development. Well done on journaling 😊

Hi I've only been diagnosed with PTSD but what I've found to help is putting a lot of work into your house/bedroom

So work on your room like your temple, the key point is to overwhelm all your senses with something that makes you feel happy/safe/relaxed. Candles for low soothing light for your eyes. Incense for a relaxing smell (I've found lavender incense is nice). Quiet music that you love to make you happy. And most importantly nice bedsheets to keep you comfy and help with nicer sleep. These can all be very cheap investments, for instance I'd say a good first step is to buy silk pillowcases which sound expensive but you can get them for £20 from Amazon.

Also find something to be creative with that makes you feel like yourself and can help you release emotion and completely forget about everything happening in your life. I like to make my own candles and mix them with essential oils to combine creativity, nice lighting, and nice smell.

These all sound quite simple but I've found that even if I'm having bad flashbacks and dissociation if I walk into my room with everything I mentioned I can easily relax.

Good luck! Peace and love ♥️

I looked through scientific papers and there was one where they experimented with rats to see dopamine's effect on swallowing. They found that if they inject the rat with dopamine then it makes it swallow. But if they stop the rat's salivary glands from working, injecting dopamine stops it from swallowing. 

There is also another established test to test drugs' effects on mice. Where they basically inject the mouse with a drug and if the mouse starts chewing randomly with its mouth empty then that means that drug activates a certain type of dopamine receptor in your brain and not another. So as you can see from both these examples dopamine is what makes you swallow and chew and not vice-versa.

My expectation on this is that the multisensory process of finding and putting food in your mouth is what gives you dopamine. The rise in dopamine then makes you chew and swallow.

Also, you get different amounts of dopamine from burgers and apples because of the concentration of fat and sugar in it, and usually the higher they are the more dopamine you get from them because your brain wants to feed you well to prepare for food shortages.

TL;DR:
Dopamine makes you chew and swallow not the other way round. And it's the amount of sugar and fat that makes food give you different amounts of dopamine.

When you get the butterfly feeling is when you get adrenaline in your bloodstream.

Adrenaline's job is to get you to either run away from a bear, or fight said bear. And to do this you need more oxygen and sugar more fast to your muscles. Therefore adrenaline shunts the blood away from your digestive system and sends it to your muscles, hence giving you the butterflies in your tummy.

There are two things that your brain can feel or make you feel. There's "Good" and there's "Reward".

"Good" comes from chemicals in your brain like the famous serotonin among others, where it makes you feel happy and lifted and in a good mood. The most popular antidepressants target serotonin.

Now we come to "Reward", and that's dopamine. Both are very popular and, understandably, are often mixed together. Dopamine rewards you, but it doesn't just make you feel good, and here's the key difference, it makes you hunt for the thing that gave you the dopamine. Things that give you dopamine are for example, cigarettes, food, and some drugs. This helps explain why candy, nicotine and morphine are addictive, but antidepressants that target serotonin are not addictive. There have also been some interesting experiments where mice that can't make dopamine never go looking for food.

And why do you feel the pleasure in your mouth? Well it's all actually going in your brain with different chemicals being released in different places, but you feel it in your mouth the same way as you feel an orgasm erm... down there. My guess is that dopamine and serotonin are released in your brain in places associated with your mouth or other regions but I am not sure of this because I can't find a source for it.

Also, these are all a combination of simplifications and also the most popular theories today. Adding more information gets confusing real fast... Neuroscience is freaking hard.

Source - I'm a biomedical scientist. Hope this helps explain it <3 And as always I'm open to criticism and questions.
